text: Are you absolutely certain we're meant to turn left after the cathedral?
target_aspect: Rising intonation on enquiry and natural vowel length in 'cathedral'.

text: Splendid, another torrential downpour right in the middle of our July picnic.
target_aspect: Subtle British sarcastic inflection on 'Splendid'.

text: Well, erm... to be completely honest, I hadn't really considered that possibility.
target_aspect: Handling of pauses, conversational disfluency 'erm', and natural phrasing.

text: Did you lock the back door?
target_aspect: Snappy, crisp turn articulation without truncation.

text: Of course I did, mate. Twice.
target_aspect: Colloquial cadence and sentence-final emphasis.

text: The committee spent three exhausting hours debating whether the proposed railway expansion through Surrey would disrupt local heritage sites or merely cause minor traffic diversions.
target_aspect: Prosodic consistency, breath pacing, and absence of pitch drift across long clauses.

text: That'll be £45.50 for the train fare, plus an extra £3.20 for the return voucher.
target_aspect: Correct pronunciation of '£' as pounds and decimal amounts.

text: The vintage sports car was auctioned off for an astonishing £124,500.
target_aspect: Handling of large sums in GBP.

text: The inquest is scheduled for the 14th of July, shortly before quarter to four in the afternoon.
target_aspect: British date format and typical time phrasing ('quarter to four').

text: Meet me outside St Pancras station at half past seven tomorrow morning.
target_aspect: British colloquial time expression 'half past seven'.

text: We drove through Gloucestershire, stopped in Worcestershire, and finished the journey near Leicester Square.
target_aspect: Non-phonetic British place name pronunciation (/ˈwʊstəʃə/, /ˈglɒstəʃə/, /ˈlɛstə/).

text: Her grandmother lives in Edinburgh, just a short stroll from the Royal Mile.
target_aspect: Correct pronunciation of Edinburgh (/ˈɛdɪnbərə/).

text: Dr. Watson met Mrs. Higgins at No. 10 Downing Street before contacting the BBC.
target_aspect: Expansion of titles and standard UK abbreviations.

text: The wind was strong enough to wind the ribbon tightly around the mast, and I read what he had lead me to.
target_aspect: Disambiguation of 'wind' (/wɪnd/ vs /waɪnd/) and 'read' (/rɛd/ vs /riːd/).

text: Thank heavens for that! I genuinely thought we'd missed the last coach home.
target_aspect: Emotional relief and expressive dynamics without screeching or clipping.

text: Honestly, could you not have warned me before making such an absurd blunder?
target_aspect: Understated irritation and indignation.

text: Don't get your knickers in a twist, it's not the end of the world, is it?
target_aspect: Colloquial idiom, tag question ('is it?') intonation.

text: Well [laughter], that certainly didn't go according to plan.
target_aspect: Handling of inline bracketed emotional cues if supported, or graceful preservation.

text: Please dispatch the parcel to Flat 4B, Kensington High Street, London W8 5SE.
target_aspect: Alphanumeric alphanumeric postcode pronunciation (W-eight five-S-E).

text: Wait a second, are you implying that—
target_aspect: Sudden stop / cutoff pacing in dialogue.

text: Precisely. Exactly what you're thinking.
target_aspect: Decisive, firm one-word opening.

text: Would you be so terribly kind as to pass the marmalade, if it's not too much trouble?
target_aspect: Excessively polite British RP phrasing and softening intonation.

text: The trail extends for 18.5 miles, rising about 450 metres above sea level.
target_aspect: Decimal numbers and unit reading.

text: Alastair and Niamh agreed to meet Siobhan at the pub on Borough High Street.
target_aspect: Phonetic rendering of traditional UK/Irish names (/ˈniːv/, /ʃɪˈvɔːn/).

text: Right then. Let's get cracking, shall we?
target_aspect: Typical British conversational sign-off and tag question.
